content: This article discusses the composition of the human body in terms of fat, bone, and muscle. It does not focus on the chemical composition of the body, which is covered elsewhere. In the context of physical fitness, body composition refers to the percentages of fat, bone, and muscle in the body. Since muscle tissue occupies less space than fat tissue, body composition, along with body weight, determines an individual's leanness. Two individuals of the same height and weight can appear very different due to variations in their body composition. The National Institute of Health recommends that a healthy adult male should have a body fat percentage between 13% and 17%. For healthy adult females, the recommended body fat percentage is between 20% and 25%. Body fat levels significantly above these ranges may indicate excess body fat. Athletes, leaner individuals, and those with higher muscle mass typically have body fat percentages lower than these recommended levels. For most athletes, optimal performance is associated with body fat percentages ranging from 7% to 19% for men and 10% to 25% for women, depending on the sport. Body composition, particularly body fat percentage, can be measured using various methods. The most common method involves the use of calipers to measure the thickness of subcutaneous fat at multiple sites on the body, such as the abdominal area, subscapular region, arms, buttocks, and thighs. These measurements are then used to estimate total body fat with an approximate margin of error of 4 percentage points. Another method is bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA), which estimates body fat by measuring the resistance of electrical flow through the body. A more accurate but less convenient method involves hydrostatic weighing, which uses a large tank of water to measure body buoyancy. Increased body fat results in greater buoyancy, while higher muscle mass causes a tendency to sink. A similar technique, known as air displacement plethysmography (ADP), uses air instead of water. In this method, the subject enters a sealed chamber that measures body volume by the displacement of air. Body volume is then combined with body weight to calculate body density, which is used to estimate body fat percentage and lean body mass (LBM) through established equations. Dual X-ray Absorptiometry (DXA) is increasingly used for clinical and research purposes to measure body composition. DXA scans provide accurate and precise measurements of bone mineral content (BMC), bone mineral density (BMD), lean tissue mass, fat tissue mass, and body fat percentage. These measurements are highly reproducible, making them ideal for monitoring pharmaceutical therapy, nutritional or exercise interventions, sports training, and other programs aimed at altering body composition. DXA scans are fast, simple, non-invasive, and expose the subject to minimal X-ray radiation, lower than that of a cross-country flight. DXA exams can provide both total body and up to 14 regional results, including specific areas such as the trunk, individual arms and legs, android, and gynoid regions. Body composition can also be estimated using advanced imaging techniques such as Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and Computed Tomography (CT). These methods provide the most precise body composition measurements available to date. As a result, many pharmaceutical companies are interested in using these techniques to assess body composition changes before and after drug therapy, particularly for drugs that may alter body composition.
